110007.text: If you looked up the little island of Tana Masa on the map you would find it just on the Equator, not far south of Sumatra; but if you were on the deck of the Kandong Bandoeng and asked its captain, J. van Toch, what he thought of this Tana Masa where you’ve just dropped anchor he would first curse for a short while and then he would tell you that it’s the dirtiest hole all the Sunda Islands, even more loathsome than Tana Bala and easily as damnable as Pini or Banyak; that the only apology for a human being that lives there — not counting these louse-ridden Bataks, of course — is a drunken commercial agent, a cross between a Cuban and a Portuguese, and an even bigger thief, pagan and pig than the whole of Cuba and the whole of the white race put together; if there’s anything in this world that’s damnable then it’s the damned life on this damned Tana Masa.

110008.text: And then, you might cautiously ask him why it is that he’s just dropped his damned anchor as if he wanted to spend three damned days here; at which he would snort in irritation and grumble something about not being so damned stupid as to sail all the way to Kandon Bandoeng just to get this damned copra or palm oil, and there’s nothing else here, but I’ve got my damned orders, and you will please be so kind as to mind your own damned business.

110009.text: And he would carry on cursing as widely and as fully as you might expect from a sea captain who was no longer young but still lively for his age.

110010.text: But if, instead of asking all sorts of impertinent questions, you left Captain J. van Toch to grumble and curse by himself you might find out something more.

110011.text: Surely it’s obvious the man needs a rest.

110012.text: Just leave him alone, he can sort out his foul mood by himself.

110015.text: “Those damned Jew-boys back in Amsterdam, all they seem to think about is pearls.

110016.text: Have a look around you; can you see any pearls?

110017.text: They say the people are crazy round here for pearls and that sort of thing.”

110018.text: At this point the captain spat in anger.

110020.text: That’s because you people always want to start a war or something.

110021.text: All you’re worried about is money.

110022.text: And then you call it a crisis.”

110023.text: For a short while, Captain J. van Toch considered whether he ought to start discussing political economics, considering that that’s all they ever do talk about nowadays.

110024.text: But it’s too hot and languid to talk about that sort of thing here, anchored off Tana Masa; so the captain merely waved his hand and grumbled: “That’s what they say, pearls!

110025.text: In Ceylon they’ve got enough pearls piled up to last them for five years, on Formosa they’ve put a ban on gathering them — and so they say to me, Captain van Toch, go and see if you can find somewhere new to gather pearls.

110026.text: Go on down to those damned little islands, you might find whole bays full of oysters down there …”

110027.text: The captain pulled out his light-blue handkerchief and blew his nose in contempt.

110028.text: “Those rats in Europe, they think there’s still something to find down here, something they don’t already know about.

110029.text: God, what a bunch of fools they are!

110030.text: Next they’ll be wanting me to look up the Bataks snouts to see if they don’t have them full of pearls.

110032.text: I know there’s a new brothel in Padang, but new pearl fisheries?

110033.text: I know these islands like my trousers, all the way from Ceylon down to that damned Clipperton Island, and if anyone thinks there’s anything new still left to find there that they can make any money out of, well good luck to them.

110034.text: Thirty years I’ve been sailing these waters, and now these fools think I’m going to discover something new!”

110035.text: This was a task so insulting it made Captain van Toch gasp.

110036.text: “Why can’t they send some green kid to find something for them if they want to gape in astonishment; but instead they expect someone to do that who knows the area as well as Captain J. van Toch … Please try and understand this.

110037.text: In Europe there might still be something left to discover; but here — people only come here to sniff out something they could eat, or rather not even to eat, to find something to buy and sell.

110038.text: If in all these damned tropics there was still something they could double the price of there’d be three commercial agents standing there waving their snotty handkerchiefs at the ships of seven countries to stop for it.

110040.text: I know about these things better than the colonial office of Her Majesty the Queen, if you’ll forgive me.”

110041.text: Captain van Toch made a great effort to overcome his righteous indignation, and after a prolonged period of exertion he was successful.

110042.text: “D’you see those two contemptible layabouts down there?

110122.text: Captain J. van Toch turned red.

110124.text: “You dirty Cuban, you think I’m afraid of these demons?

110125.text: We’ll see about that,” he said as he stood up with all the mass of his honest two hundred pounds.

110126.text: “I’m not going to waste my time with you here, not when I’ve got business to attend to.

110127.text: But just remember this; the Dutch colonies don’t have any demons in them; even if there are in the French.

110129.text: And now call the mayor of this damned Kampong over to speak to me.”

110130.text: It did not take long to find the aforementioned dignitary; he was squatting down beside the half-casts shop chewing sugar cane.

110131.text: He was an elderly man, naked, but a lot thinner than mayors usually are in Europe.

110132.text: Some way behind him, keeping the appropriate distance, the entire village was also squatting, complete with women and children.

110135.text: “Now listen to this, son, I need a few big, strong, powerful lads to go out on a fishing trip with me.

110138.text: The half-cast translated this and the mayor nodded his head to show he understood; then he turned round to face the wider audience and said something to them, clearly meeting with great success.

110141.text: So tell him were going to fish for clams in Devil Bay.”

110158.text: Captain J. van Toch began to turn blue.

110160.text: The half-cast translated what he had said, as far as his vocabulary was able; and then he once again translated the Bataks long, but objective, verdict back to the captain.

110161.text: “They say they might be willing to relinquish taking you to court, Captain, if you pay a fine into the hands of the local authorities.

110164.text: Captain van Toch’s complexion began to break out in purple blotches.

110165.text: First he offered to murder all the Bataks in the world, then the offer went down to giving them all three hundred good kickings, and finally he agreed to content himself with stuffing the mayor and putting him on display in the colonial museum in Amsterdam; for their part, the Bataks went down from two hundred rupees to an iron pump with a wheel, and finally insisted on no more than that the captain give the mayor his petrol cigarette lighter as a token.

110166.text: (“Give it to him, Captain,” urged the half-cast of Cubanese and Portuguese, “I’ve got three cigarette lighters in my store, even if they don’t have wicks.”)

110167.text: Thus, peace was restored on Tana Masa; but Captain J. van Toch now knew that the dignity of the white race was at stake.

110168.text: That afternoon a boat set out from the Dutch ship, Kandon Bandoeng, with the following crew: Captain J. van Toch, Jensen the Swede, Gudmundson the Icelander, Gillemainen the Finn, and two Sinhalese pearl fishers.

110169.text: The boat headed straight for Devil Bay.

110170.text: At three o’clock, when the tide was at its highest, the captain stood on the shore, the boat was out watching for sharks about a hundred meters offshore, and both the Sinhalese divers were waiting, knife in hand, for the signal to jump into the water.

110171.text: “Now you go in,” the captain told the farther of the two naked savages.

110172.text: The Sinhalese jumped into the water, waded out a few paces and then dived.

110173.text: The captain looked at his watch.

110174.text: After four minutes and twenty seconds a brown head emerged to his left, about sixty meters away; with a strange, desperate shudder which seemed at the same time as if paralysed, the Sinhalese clawed at the rocks, in one hand he had the knife, in the other some pearl bearing oysters.

110178.text: The Sinhalese was still slithering up the rock, unable to speak with the horror of it.

110181.text: “Saheb, Saheb,” said the Sinhalese as he sank down on the beach, gasping for breath.

110187.text: He pressed his fist into his eye.

110189.text: “Show me those oysters,” the captain ordered him, and began to open one with the knife.

110190.text: Inside, there was a small, perfect pearl.

110192.text: The Sinhalese drew another three oysters out from the bag he had hanging round his neck.

110193.text: “There are oysters down there, Captain, but they are guarded by these demons …

110194.text: They were watching me as I cut them off …”

110195.text: The curls on his head stuck out with shock.

110197.text: The captain opened the oysters; two of them were empty and in the third there was a pearl the size of a pea, as round as a drop of mercury.

110198.text: Captain van Toch looked at the pearl and then at the Sinhalese collapsed on the ground.

110199.text: “won’t you,” he said hesitantly, “dive in there one more time?”

110200.text: Without a word, the Sinhalese shook his head.

110201.text: Captain J. van Toch felt a strong urge to castigate and shout at the Sinhalese; but to his surprise he found that he was speaking quietly and almost gently: “Don’t you worry, lad.

110202.text: And what did they look like, these … demons?”

110203.text: “Like little children,” said the Sinhalese with a sigh.

110204.text: “They have a tail, Captain, and they’re about this high,” indicating about one meter twenty above the ground.

110205.text: “They stood all around me and watched what I was doing … a sort of circle of them …”

110208.text: Captain van Toch thought for a while.

110209.text: “And what about when they blink; was it with their lower eyelid or what?”

110210.text: “I don’t know, Captain,” the Sinhalese croaked.

110211.text: “There are ten thousand of them there!”

110212.text: The captain looked round to find the other Sinhalese; he stood about fifty meters away, waiting without interest with his hands crossed over on his shoulders; perhaps because when a person is naked he has nowhere else to put his hands than on his own shoulders.

110213.text: The captain gave him a silent signal and the gaunt Sinhalese jumped into the water.

110214.text: After three minutes and fifty seconds he re-emerged, clawing at the slippery rocks.

110215.text: “Come on, hurry up,” the captain shouted, but then he began to look more carefully and soon he himself was jumping and clambering over the rocks to the Sinhalese; no-one would have thought that a body like that could jump so nimbly.

110216.text: At the last moment he caught hold of the Sinhalese hand and pulled him breathless from the water.

110217.text: Then he lay him on the rock and wiped the sweat off his brow.

110218.text: The Sinhalese lay without moving; his shin had been scraped and the bone underneath was exposed, clearly he had injured it on some rock, but he was otherwise unhurt.

110219.text: The captain raised the man’s eyelid; all he could see was the white.

110220.text: There was no sign of any oysters or the knife.

110238.text: A strip of white appeared once more in the Sinhalese eyes.

110239.text: Captain J. van Toch, with unexpected liveliness, slapped him on both cheeks with his full hand to bring him back to consciousness.

110240.text: “Thanks, Saheb,” the gaunt Sinhalese sighed, and the pupils re-appeared in his eyes.

110282.text: He did not return to the village until dawn; said not a word to anyone but merely had himself taken back to the ship, where he locked himself in his cabin until evening.

110299.text: Then, together with Gudmundson the Icelander, he took the little boat and rowed down to Devil Bay.

110300.text: They stayed in the boat behind the rocks and waited to see what would happen.

110301.text: The captain came across the bay and seemed to be waiting for someone; he stopped for a while and called out something like ts-ts-ts.

110302.text: “Look at this,” said Gudmundson, pointing to the sea which now glittered red and gold in the sunset.

110304.text: “Oh God,” grumbled Jensen, “there are sharks here!”

110305.text: When, shortly afterwards, one of the little scythes submerged, a tail swished out above the water and created a violent eddy.

110306.text: At this, Captain J. van Toch on the shore began to jump up and down in fury, issued a gush of curses and threatened the sharks with his fist.

110307.text: Then the short tropical twilight was over and the light of the moon shone over the island; Jensen took the oars and rowed the boat to within a furlong of the shore.

110308.text: Now the captain was sitting on a rock calling ts-ts-ts.

110309.text: Nearby something moved, but it was not possible to see exactly what.

110310.text: It looks like a seal, thought Jensen, but seals don’t move like that.

110311.text: It came out of the water between the rocks and pattered along the beach, swaying from side to side like a penguin.

110312.text: Jensen quietly rowed in and stopped half a furlong away from the captain.

110315.text: Just then the raised oar slipped out of Jensen’s hand and fell in the water with a splash.

110316.text: The captain lifted his head, got up and walked about thirty paces into the water; there was a sudden flashing and banging; the captain was shooting with his browning in the direction of the boat.

110317.text: Almost simultaneously there was a rustling and a splashing in the bay as, with a whirl of activity, it seemed as if a thousand seals were jumping into the water; but Jensen and Gudmundson were already pressing on the oars and driving the boat so hard that it swished through the water until it was behind the nearest corner.

110318.text: When they got back to the ship they said not a word to anyone.

110319.text: The northern races know how to keep silent.

110320.text: In the morning the captain returned; he was angry and unhappy, but said nothing.

110321.text: Only, when Jensen helped him on board both men gave each other a cold and inquisitive look.

110331.text: At the same time he sent a telegram asking for his annual leave.

110336.text: He was also quite startling in appearance, as both hands, his breast and his legs were heavily scarred from contact with shark skin and his nose and ears were decorated with shark teeth.

110338.text: With this Dayak, Captain J. van Toch set off back to the island of Tana Masa.

110340.text: As far as the newspapers were concerned, it was the sort of hot day when nothing, absolutely nothing, happens, when no politics is done and there aren’t even any tensions in Europe; but it is just on days like this that newspaper readers, lying in an agony of boredom on the beaches or in the sparse shade of trees, demoralised by the heat, the view, the quiet of the countryside and all that makes up their healthy and simple life on holiday, hope in vain to find to find something in the newspapers, something that will be new and refreshing, some murder, some war or some earthquake, in short, anything; and when they are disappointed they throw the paper down and declare in irritation that there is nothing there, nothing whatsoever, that it is not worth reading and they will stop buying a newspaper in future.

110341.text: Meanwhile in the editorial office, there are five or six people left by themselves, as their colleagues are also all on holiday, who throw the paper down in irritation and complain that there is nothing there, nothing whatsoever.

112511.text: For the scientist, the mysteries of Andrias Scheuchzeri were quite different: where, for instance, did it come from; where had it been throughout entire geological periods; how did it remain unknown for so long when reports of it now were coming in from all tropical parts of the Pacific Ocean.

112512.text: It seems to have been multiplying at an exceptional speed in recent times; how had it acquired such amazing vitality while still in a primitive triassic form, and how had it remained entirely hidden until recently, existing, most likely, in extremely isolated geographic pockets?

112513.text: Had there been a change of some sort in this ancient newt that brought biological advantages so that this rare vestige from the miocene period was given a new and remarkably effective period of existence?

112514.text: In this case it would not be out of the question for Andrias not only to multiply but even to evolve into a better form, and that human science would have the unique opportunity to assist in some of the enormous changes to be undergone by at least one animal species.

112515.text: The ability of Andrias Scheuchzeri to grunt a few dozen words and learn a few phrases — which the lay public perceives as a sign of some kind of intelligence — is no great wonder from a scientific point of view; but the power and vigour with which it shows its ability to survive, bringing it so suddenly and so successfully back to life after spending so long in abeyance, in a retarded state of development and nearly extinct, is no less than miraculous.

112516.text: There are some unusual circumstances to be considered here: Andrias Scheuchzeri is the only species of newt living in the sea and — even more remarkable — the only newt to be found in the area from Ethiopia to Australasia, the Lemuria of ancient myths.

112517.text: Could we not almost say that Nature now wishes to add another form of animal to the world by a precipitate acceleration of the development of a single species, a species which she has so far neglected or has so far been unable to bring fully to life?

112518.text: Moreover: it would be odd if the giant newts of Japan and those of the Alleghan Islands did not have some connecting link in the regions of the ocean lying between them.

112519.text: If Andrias had not been found it would have been necessary to postulate its existence in the very places where it was found; it would simply be needed to fill the space where, according to the geographic and developmental context, it must have been since ancient times.

112520.text: Be that as it may, the learned professor’s article concluded, this evolutionary resurrection of a miocene newt cannot fail to fill us all with as much reverence as astonishment at the Genius of Evolution on our planet which is clearly still far from ending its creative task.

112521.text: This article was published despite the tacit, but definite, view of the editors that a learned article of this sort does not belong in a newspaper.

112522.text: Soon afterwards, Professor Uher received a letter from one of its readers:

112524.text: Last year I bought a house on the town square in Čáslav.

112525.text: While examining the house I found a box in the attic containing some rare and very old papers which were clearly of a scientific nature.

112526.text: They included two years’ issues of Hýbel’s journal, Hyllos for the years 1821 and 22, Jan Svatopluk Presl’s Mammals, Vojtěch Sedláček’s Nature of Physics, nineteen years’ issues of the general educational publication, Progress, and thirteen years’ issues of the Czech Museum Magazine.

112527.text: Inserted next to Presls translation of Cuviers Discussion of Upheavals in the Earths Crust (from 1834)

112528.text: I found and article torn out of some old newspaper about some remarkable lizards.

112529.text: When I read your distinguished article about these mysterious newts I was reminded of this box and brought it back down.

112530.text: I think it might be of some interest to you, and I am therefore, as an enthusiastic nature lover and great admirer of your works, sending its contents to you.

112533.text: The cutting included with this letter bore neither title nor date; but the style and spelling suggest it came from the third or fourth decade of the nineteenth century; it was accordingly so yellow and decayed that it was very hard to read.

112534.text: Professor Uher was about to throw it into the bin but he was somehow impressed by the age of this piece of printed paper; he began to read; and after a short time he exclaimed “My God!” and readjusted his glasses.

112535.text: The cutting bore the following text:

112537.text: We read in one of the newspapers published overseas that a certain captain, the commander of an English man of war, having returned from a voyage to distant lands, has brought back reports concerning some rather remarkable lizards which he encountered on a minor island in the Australian ocean.

112538.text: On this island, we are told, there is to be found a salt water lake which has neither access to the open sea nor any other means of approach not involving great exertions and difficulties.

112539.text: It was this salt lake that the aforementioned captain and his medical officer had chosen for their recreation when from it emerged some unfamiliar animals.

112540.text: These animals greatly resembled lizards, their means of locomotion, however, was on two legs similar to human beings.

112541.text: In size they were comparable with a sea lion or seal, and once on shore they began to move around in their peculiar manner, giving the impression of a charming and elegant dance.

112542.text: The captain and his medical officer were successful in obtaining one of these animals by means of their guns and inform us that their bodies are of a slimey character, without hair and without anything resembling scales, so that they bear some resemblance to salamanders.

112543.text: The following day, when they returned to the same spot, they were obliged immediately to depart again because of the overpowering stench, and they instructed their divers to hunt all the newts in the lake with their nets, by which means all but a few of the animals were annihilated, leaving no more than two examples which were taken on board the ship.

112544.text: Upon establishing that their bodies contained some kind of poison and the skin was burning to the touch in a way that resembled the sting of a nettle, the animals were placed in barrels of salt water in order that they might be returned to england alive.

112545.text: However, while the ship was near the island of sumatra the captive lizards were successful in making their way from the barrels, opening without any assistance one of the windows of a lower deck, throwing themselves into the sea, and making their escape under cover of darkness.

112546.text: According to the testimony of officers and ratings on board the ship these animals were remarkably odd and sly, walking as they did on their hind legs, and issuing strange barking and squelching sounds.

112547.text: They seemed however to present no danger to man.

112548.text: It would seem appropriate from the preceding to give them the name ‘anthroposaurus’.

112550.text: “My God!” repeated the professor in some excitement, “why is there no date or title on this cutting?

112551.text: And what was this foreign newspaper named by this certain commander and what English ship was this?

112552.text: What was the small island in the Australian Ocean?

112553.text: couldn’t these people have been a bit more precise and a bit more, well, a bit more scientific?

112554.text: This is a historic document, it’s priceless …”

112555.text: A small island in the Australian Ocean, yes.

112557.text: It sounds like a coral island, an atoll with a salt lagoon, difficult of access: just the sort of place a prehistoric species of this sort might survive, isolated from the evolutional developments of other species and undisturbed in a natural reservation.

112558.text: Of course they wouldn’t have been able to multiply because of the lack of food in the lake.

112559.text: It’s obvious, the professor said to himself.

112560.text: An animal similar to a lizard, but without scales and walking on its hind legs like a man: it could only be Andrias Scheuchzeri, or another newt closely related to it.

112561.text: Supposing it was the same Andrias.

112562.text: Supposing those damned divers in that lagoon wiped them out and just the one pair were taken alive onto that ship; a pair that escaped into the sea by Sumatra.

112563.text: That would mean right on the Equator, in conditions highly favourable for life and with unlimited food.

112564.text: Could it be that this change of environment gave this miocene newt a powerful new evolutionary impulse?

112565.text: It was certainly used to salt water: lets suppose its new home was a calm, enclosed bay with plenty of food; what would happen then?

112566.text: The newts transposed into an environment with optimal conditions, having enormous vigour; their population would burgeon.

112567.text: That’s it, the scientist declared joyfully.

112568.text: The newts would start to develop uncontrollably; they would throw themselves into life like mad; they would multiply at an amazing rate because their eggs and their tadpoles would have no particular enemies in the new environment.

112569.text: They would colonise one island after another — it’s only strange that some islands have been overlooked.

112570.text: In all other respects it’s typical of migration patterns in pursuit of food — and that raises the question of why they didn’t develop earlier.

112571.text: Could it be to do with the fact that there is no known species of newt in the area between Ethiopia and Australia?

112572.text: Or rather hasn’t been until now.

112573.text: Could there have been some development in this area in the miocene period which was unfavourable for newts?

112575.text: Could there have been some particular predator which simply hunted the newts to extinction?

112576.text: Just on a single small island, with an isolated lake, is where the miocene newt survived — albeit at the price of its evolution coming to a halt.

112577.text: It was like a compressed spring waiting to be released.

112578.text: It’s not even out of the question that Nature had its own great plans for this newt, it might have developed even further and further, higher and higher, who knows how high …

112579.text: (At this thought, Professor Uher shuddered slightly; who knows that Andrias Scheuchzeri was not meant to be the human beings of the miocene!)

112581.text: This undeveloped animal suddenly finds itself in a new environment offering boundless promise; a compressed spring waiting to be released.

112582.text: Andrias will have thrown itself into its development with so much miocene vigour and enthusiasm, so much élan vital!

112583.text: So much frenzy to catch up on the thousands and millions of years during which evolution passed it by!

112584.text: Is it at all possible it would be content with just the level of development it has reached today?

112585.text: It would show just the sort of upsurge we have seen — or else it’s just on the threshhold of its evolution and getting ready to rise — and who can say where it will go!

112586.text: These were the thoughts and observation that Professor Vladimír Uher wrote down about this yellowed cutting from an ancient publication, shaking with the intellectual enthusiasm of a discoverer.

112587.text: I must publish it in the newspapers, he said to himself, as nobody ever reads scientific publications.

112588.text: Let everyone know what enormous events Nature has in store for us!

112589.text: I will entitle it Do Newts have a Future?

112590.text: Only, the editor of the Peoples Press looked at Professor Uher’s article and shook his head.

112592.text: I think our readers have had it up to their necks with these newts.

112593.text: It’s about time we found something else to write about.

112594.text: And a scientific article such as this doesn’t belong in the papers anyway.

112595.text: As a result, the article about the development and prospects of the newts never did appear.

112597.text: President G.H. Bondy rang the bell and stood up.

112598.text: “Gentlemen,” he began, “I have the honour of opening this extraordinary general meeting of the Pacific Export Company.

112599.text: I would like to welcome everyone here and thank them for the contribution they make.”

112600.text: “I also,” he continued with some emotion, “have the sad duty of giving you some tragic news.

112601.text: Captain Jan van Toch is no longer with us.

112602.text: Our founder, if I can call him that, the father of the great idea of establishing commercial contact with thousands of islands in the far Pacific, our first captain and enthusiastic fellow worker has died.

112603.text: He passed away at the start of this year on board our ship, Šárka, not far from Fanning Island after suffering a stroke while engaged in his duty.”

112604.text: (Bet he made a Hell of a fuss, poor man, thought Mister Bondy fleetingly.)

112605.text: “Let us now all stand up in honour of this mans bright memory.”

112606.text: All present stood up with a scraping and clattering of chairs and then remained in formal silence, all of them united in the hope that this general meeting wouldn’t last too long.

112607.text: (Poor Vantoch, my friend, thought G.H. Bondy with sincere emotion.

112608.text: What does he look like now?

112609.text: I expect they put him on a plank and threw him into the sea — what a splash that must have made!

112610.text: He was certainly a man of great honour, and had such blue eyes … )

112611.text: “Thank you, gentlemen,” he added briefly, “for showing such piety in memory of my personal friend, Captain van Toch.

112612.text: I now invite our director, Mister Volavka, to inform you of the economic prospects for PEC over the coming year.

112613.text: None of these figures are yet certain but I hope you won’t expect them too have changed too much by the end of the year.

112615.text: “Good afternoon,” Mister Volavka began, and off he went.

112616.text: “The state of the pearl market is very unsatisfactory.

112617.text: Pearl production last year was nearly twelve times higher than in 1925, which itself was a very good year, but now the price of pearls has begun a catastrophic decline, by as much as sixty five percent.

112618.text: Management has decided, therefore, not to put any of this years pearl harvest on the market and they will be kept in storage until demand has risen again.

112619.text: Unfortunately, pearls went out of fashion last autumn, clearly because they had sunk so low in price.

112620.text: Our Amsterdam branch has, at present, more than two hundred thousand pearls in stock which, for the time being, are next to impossible to sell.

112621.text: “At the same time,” Mister Volavka purred on, “there has been a marked reduction in the number of pearls found this year.

112622.text: Many fisheries have had to be abandoned because production was too low.

112623.text: Fisheries discovered just two or three years ago seem to be more or less exhausted.

112624.text: It is for this reason that the management had decided to turn its attention to other fruits of the sea such as coral and shellfish.

112625.text: There has been some success in stimulating the market for coral jewellery and other ornaments, but even here coral from Italy is achieving greater success than that from the Pacific.

112626.text: The management is also studying the possibility of intensive fishing in the deepest parts of the Pacific Ocean, where the main consideration is how to transport the fish from the Pacific to the European and American markets; results and findings so far are not very encouraging.

112627.text: “On the other hand,” the director went on, his voice rising slightly, “our relatively high turnover suggests it might be profitable to diversify into other activities such as the export of textiles, enamel ware, wireless sets and gloves to the Pacific.

112629.text: This business would be amenable to further development; although this year it is already showing a slight loss.

112630.text: there is of course no question of PEC paying any dividend to its shareholders at the end of the year; and the management would like to announce in advance that, on this occasion, it will renounce any commissions and bonuses …”

112631.text: There was a painful silence in the room.

112632.text: (It must have been like this on Fanning Island, thought G.H. Bondy.

112633.text: He died a true sailor, Vantoch.

112635.text: It’s a pity a decent chap like that had to die.

112636.text: And he wasn’t even that old … he was no older than I am … )

112637.text: Dr. Hubka stood up to speak; and the minutes of the extraordinary general meeting of the Pacific Export Company continued thus:

112638.text: Dr. Hubka asks whether the PEC might go into liquidation

112639.text: G.H. Bondy replies that management has decided to wait for further suggestions in that matter.

112640.text: Monsieur Louis Bonenfant urges that pearl production should have been done under the supervision of permanent representatives, continuously on site at fisheries, who would check whether pearls were being gathered with enough vigour and specialist skill.

112641.text: Mr. Volavka, director, observes that this has been considered, but it was thought that this would result in excessive administration costs.

112642.text: There would need to be at least three hundred agents on the payroll; there was also the question of how these agents would themselves be supervised to ensure that all pearls found were passed on to the company.

112643.text: M.H. Brinkelaer asks whether the newts can be relied on to pass on all the pearls found by them, and whether they do not dispose of them to somebody not connected with the company.

112644.text: G.H. Bondy observes that this is the first time the newts have been mentioned in public.

112645.text: It has been a rule in this place, up till now, not to mention any details of how the gathering of pearls is carried out.

112646.text: He points out that it was for this reason that the inconspicuous title of Pacific Export Company chosen.

112647.text: M.H. Brinkelaer asks whether it is unacceptable, in this place, to talk about matters which affect the interests of the company, and which moreover have long been known by the general public.

112648.text: G.H. Bondy replies that it is not unacceptable, but it is unprecedented.

112649.text: He welcomes that fact that it is now possible to speak openly.

112650.text: In reply to Mister Brinkelaer’s first question, he can state that as far as he knows there is no reason to doubt the total honesty of the newts and their willingness to work at gathering pearls and corals.

112651.text: We must however reckon on known pearl fisheries becoming effectively exhausted in the near future.

112652.text: Where new fisheries are concerned, it was on a journey to find islands which are so far unexploited that our unforgettable colleague, Captain van Toch, died.

112653.text: It has so far been found impossible to find another man with the same experience and the same unshakeable honesty and love for his work to replace him.

112654.text: Colonel D.W. Bright fully acknowledges the services rendered by the late Captain van Toch.

112655.text: He points out, however, that the captain, whose loss we all regret, did show too much concern for the comfort of the aforementioned newts.

112657.text: It was not necessary, for instance, to provide the news with knives and other equipment of such high quality as the late van Toch did.

112658.text: There was no need, for instance, to give them so much food.

112659.text: There is scope for substantial reductions in the costs associated with the maintenance of the newts and in this way raise the net income of the company.

112661.text: Vice-president J. Gilbert agrees with Colonel Bright, but points out that that was not possible while Captain van Toch was still alive.

112662.text: Captain van Toch insisted that he had his personal obligations towards the newts.

112663.text: There were various reasons why it would have been inadvisable to even suggest neglecting the old mans wishes in this respect.

112664.text: Kurt von Frisch asks whether the newts could not be employed in some other way that might be more profitable than pearl fishing.

112665.text: Their natural, one could say beaver-like, talent for building weirs and other underwater constructions should be taken into account.

112666.text: They could perhaps be put to use in deepening harbours, building piers and performing other technical tasks underwater.

112667.text: G.H. Bondy states that management is actively engaged in this consideration; there are some great possibilities in this respect.

112668.text: He states that the company now owns nearly six million newts; if we consider that one pair of newts might have a hundred tadpoles in any given year the company could well have three hundred million newts at its disposal by this time next year; in ten years the number would be astronomical.

112669.text: G.H. Bondy asks what the company intends to do with this enormous number of newts, when the newt farms are already over-populated and, because of a lack of natural foodstuffs, it has been found necessary to feed the newts with copra, potatoes, maize and similar.

112670.text: K. von Frisch asks whether the newts are edible.

112672.text: Nor do their hides have any use.

112673.text: M. Bonenfant asks management what they now intend to do.

112674.text: G.H. Bondy (standing): “Gentlemen, we convened this extraordinary general meeting in order publicly to draw your attention to the extremely unfavourable prospects of our company which — I hope you will allow me to remind you of this — has proudly paid returns of twenty to twenty-three percent over recent years as well as having well funded reserves and low costs.

112675.text: We stand now at a turning point; the way of doing business which has proved itself so well over recent years is now practically at an end; we have no choice but to find new ways.”

112677.text: “I could even say it is a sign from fate that our excellent friend and captain, J. van Toch, left us just at this time.

112678.text: Our romantic, beautiful — I could even say absurd — trading in pearls was always closely connected with him.

112679.text: I consider this to be the closing chapter in our business; it had its, so to speak, exotic charm, but it was never suitable for modern times.

112680.text: Gentlemen, pearls could never be the concern of a large company which needs to be cohesive horizontally and vertically.

112681.text: For me personally, this affair with pearls was never more than a minor distraction.”

112682.text: (Discomfiture) “Yes gentlemen; but a minor distraction which brought substantial profits to me and to you.

112683.text: At the start of our business these newts also had a kind of, shall I say, charm of the new.

112684.text: Three hundred million newts will not have much charm about them.”

112686.text: “I spoke earlier about finding new ways of moving forward.

112687.text: While my good friend, Captain van Toch, was still alive there was no question of giving our affairs any other character than that which could be called the Captain van Toch style.”

112689.text: “Because, gentlemen, I have too much good taste to mix one style with another.

112690.text: I would say that the style of Captain van Toch was that of a romantic adventurer.

112691.text: It was the style of Jack London, Joseph Conrad and others of that ilk.

112693.text: I do not deny that he charmed me with this style of his, but since his death we no longer have the right to continue with an epic tale which is adventurous and juvenile.

112694.text: We have before us not a new chapter but a new conception, gentlemen, it is a job for an imagination which is new and fundamentally different.”

112695.text: (You speak as if this were all just a story in a novel!)

112697.text: I take an artists interest in business.

112698.text: Without a sense of art it is impossible ever to think of something new.

112699.text: We need to be poets if we are to keep the world moving.”

112702.text: “Gentlemen, I am sorry to be closing this chapter, the chapter we might call the van Toch era; an era in which we made use of the child-like and adventurous side that we all have.

112703.text: The time has come now to bring this fairy story of pearls and coral fisheries to an end.

112705.text: And the question is, what now?”

112707.text: “Alright gentlemen: please take out pen and paper and write this down.

112711.text: That makes three hundred million, doesn’t it.

112713.text: Now that’s fifteen thousand million, yes?

112714.text: And now gentlemen, please be so kind as to tell me what, in three years time, were going to do with fifteen thousand million newts.

112715.text: How are we to employ them, how are we going to feed them, and so on.”

112717.text: “Yes, but don’t you think that would be a pity?

112718.text: Have you not thought that every new newt is a new business opportunity, a new unit of labour waiting to be put to use?

112719.text: Gentlemen, with six million newts we can still make business of some sort.

112720.text: With three hundred million it will be somewhat harder.

112721.text: But gentlemen, fifteen thousand million newts is something quite inconceivable.

112722.text: The newts will devour the company.

112725.text: It was you who started all this business with the newts!)

112727.text: “And I fully accept that responsibility, gentlemen.

112728.text: Anyone who wishes to can dispose of his shares in the Pacific Export Company immediately.

112729.text: I am quite willing to pay for them …”

112733.text: Chairman calls for ten minute pause)

112735.text: Expresses pleasure at high rate of increase of newts, and with it the rate of increase of company assets.

112736.text: But, gentlemen, it would of course be sheer madness to breed them without regard for the need; suggests on behalf of shareholders that if the company cannot find suitable work for them itself they should be simply sold as working force to whoever wishes to undertake any work on or under water.

112738.text: The cost of feeding a newt is no more than a few centimes; if a pair of newts is sold for, say, a hundred francs, and the working life of a newt is no more than, say, one year, then any investor would see a very good return.

112740.text: J. Gilbert indicates that newts reach ages much higher than one year; we do not yet have enough experience with them to say how long they actually live.

112741.text: H. Brinkelaer modifies his suggestion; the price of a pair of newts should be set at three hundred francs.

112742.text: S. Weissberger asks what sort of work the newts are actually capable of.

112743.text: Mr. Volavka, director: with their natural instincts and their exceptional technical training, the newts would be especially suited to the construction of weirs, embankments and breakwaters, to the deepening of harbours and channels, clearing shallow waters and removal of sediments, and to freeing water channels; they could reinforce and maintain shorelines, extend sea defences, and so on.

112744.text: For work of this sort they would operate in groups of hundreds or thousands of individuals; in projects on this large a scale, where not even modern plant and machinery could be considered, there would be no other way of performing the task at such low cost.

112747.text: Dr. Hubka objects that by selling newts that might find new places to reproduce the company might lose its monopoly on the animals.

112748.text: He suggests the newts be merely rented out to businesses engaged in water works as properly trained and qualified working units with the stipulation that any tadpoles created will continue to be the property of PEC.

112749.text: Mr. Volavka, director, points out that it would not be possible to supervise millions or even thousands of millions of newts in the water, let alone their tadpoles; many newts have already been misappropriated for zoos and menageries.

112750.text: Col. D.W. Bright: Only male newts should be sold or rented out so that they would not be able to reproduce outside the farms and incubators belonging to the company.

112751.text: Mr. Volavka, director: It is not possible to assert that newt farms are the property of the company.

112752.text: A piece of the sea floor cannot be owned or rented.

112753.text: The question of who the newts belong to, if for instance they are living in the surface waters of Her Majesty the Queen of Holland, is very unclear, legally speaking, and could lead to many disputes.

112755.text: In most cases we don’t even have any guaranteed fishing rights; in fact, gentlemen, we established our newt farms in the Pacific islands without any legal right to do so.

112757.text: J. Gilbert, responding to Colonel Bright, says that experience so far showed that male newts kept in isolation become lethargic and unwilling to work; they are lazy, apathetic and often die from stress.

112758.text: Von Frisch asks whether newts to be sold could not be castrated or sterilised beforehand.

112759.text: J. Gilbert: That would incur too many costs; there simply is no way for us to prevent newts from procreating after they have been sold.

112760.text: S. Weissberger, asks, as a member of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, that if any newts are to be sold it should be done humanely and in a way that would not offend people’s sensibilities.

112761.text: J. Gilbert thanks him for raising the subject; it is understood that the newts would be caught and transported only by trained personnel under proper supervision.

112762.text: It is not, of course, possible to be sure how the newts will be treated by the businesses that buy them.

112763.text: S. Weissberger declares that he is satisfied with the assurances given by Vice-President Gilbert.

112765.text: G.H. Bondy: “Gentlemen, we have, from now on, to abandon any idea of having a monopoly on newts.

112766.text: Unfortunately, under current regulations, we are not able to take out a patent on them.”

112768.text: “We can and must do business with newts in a way that’s fundamentally different from the way we have been up till now; and it is essential that our approach to business is fundamentally different and on a far bigger scale.”

112770.text: “And there are many things, gentlemen, that need to be agreed beforehand.

112771.text: Management suggest the creation of a new, vertically organised trust under the name Salamander Syndicate.

112772.text: Besides our company, the members of the newt syndicate would consist of certain major companies and strong financial groups; there is one company, for instance, that would be engaged in manufacturing special, patented metal tools for the newts …”

112774.text: “Yes, that’s right, MEAS is the company I have in mind.

112775.text: There will also be a cartel of companies in the field of chemicals and foodstuffs, manufacturing cheap, patented feed for the newts; there will be a group of transport companies, making use of experience already gained to patent special hygienic tanks for transporting the newts; a block of insurance companies to cover the newts against risk of death or injury during transportation or at the workplace; other interested concerns in the fields of industry, export and finance which, for legal reasons, we are not able to mention by name at this stage.

112776.text: Suffice it to say, gentlemen, that at the start of business the syndicate would have four hundred millions pounds sterling at its disposal.”

112778.text: “This file, my friends, is already full of contracts and all they need now is a signature for the creation of one of the biggest commercial organisations of modern times.

112779.text: All that is asked of you by the management, gentlemen is that you give them the authority to establish this gigantic concern whose task will be to cultivate and employ the newts in the best possible way.”

112781.text: “Gentlemen, please bear in mind the advantages a collaboration of this sort could bring.

112782.text: The Newt Syndicate would provide more than just newts, it would also provide equipment and food for the newts such as maize, carbohydrates, beef fat and sugar for thousands of millions of well fed animals; then there would be transport, insurance, veterinary needs and everything at the lowest rate guaranteed for us if not by a monopoly then at least by being in a dominant position over any other potential rival that might want to deal in newts.

112783.text: Just let them try it, gentlemen; they won’t be in competition with us for long.”

112786.text: The Newt syndicate would provide all kinds of building material for underwater work performed by the newts; for this reason we have the support also of heavy industry, cement works, the stone and timber industries …” (You still don’t know how the newts are going to work!)

112787.text: “Gentlemen, at this very moment there are twelve thousand newts at work in Saigon building new docks, basins and jetties.”

112843.text: The Sex Life Of The Newts.

112844.text: One of mans favourite activities is to imagine how the world might be in the distant future, what technical wonders will have been perfected, what social problems solved, how far science and civil organisation will have progressed, and so on.

112845.text: But however much improved, progressed or at least more technically perfect these utopias are, they never fail to take a lively interest in the question of how one of the most ancient of institutions might be.

112846.text: Sex, reproduction, love, marriage, family, the status of women and so on are as popular now as they have always been.

112847.text: Consider, in this respect, the works of Paul Adam, HG.

112848.text: Wells, Aldous Huxley and many others.

112849.text: Taking his example from these authors, and considering that he has already begun to speculate of the future of our planet, the present author regards it as his duty to speculate on what the sexual behaviour of the newts will be.

112850.text: He will settle the matter now so that he will not have to return to it later.

112851.text: In its basic outlines, the sex life of Andrias Scheuchzeri is, of course, no different from that of other tailed amphibians; there is no copulation in the proper sense of the word, the female carries the ova through several stages of their development, the fertilised ova develop into tadpoles in the water and so on; this is something that can be found in any primer of biology.

112852.text: So let us refer then to just a few peculiarities which have been observed in Andrias Scheuchzeri.

112853.text: According to the account given by H. Bolte, the male and female come together in early April; the male will usually remain with just one female throughout any one mating season, and for a period of several days will never leave her side.

112854.text: He will take no sustenance during this period, whereas the female will evince a voracious appetite.

112855.text: The male will pursue the female in the water and attempt to keep his head closely beside hers.

112856.text: If he is successful in this, then he will position his paw in front of her snout in order to prevent escape.

112858.text: In this way, with male and female in contact only at the head while their bodies form an angle of approximately thirty degrees, the two animals will float motionless side by side in the water.

112859.text: After a short time has elapsed, the male will begin to convulse with sufficient vigour for their two bodies to collide; after which he will again become stiff, his limbs extended to each side, and touching only the head of his chosen mate with his paw.

112860.text: During this, the female shows a total indifference apart from eating whatever comes within range.

112861.text: This, if we may call it thus, kissing lasts several days; at times the female will pull herself away in pursuit of food, at which the male will pursue in a state of clear agitation if not fury.

112862.text: Eventually the female ceases to show further resistance or attempt to remove herself from the male and the couple will remain floating motionless, resembling a pair of black logs attached to each other in the water.

112863.text: The body of the male will then begin to undergo cramps and convulsions, during which he will discharge large amounts of somewhat sticky foam into the water, immediately after which he will abandon the female and climb away between the rocks and stones in a state of extreme exhaustion; during this period it is possible for the observer to cut off a leg or tail without his showing any kind of defensive reaction.

112864.text: The female will remain for some time in her stiff and motionless posture; she will then show vigorous movement and discharge from her cloaca a chain of eggs inside a gelatinous covering, making frequent use of her rear limbs to assist this process in the way seen among toads.

112865.text: The eggs number between forty and fifty and hang from the female’s body.

112866.text: She will swim with them to a safe place and attach them to seaweed, algae or simply to a rock.

112867.text: After a period of ten days, the female will bear another litter of twenty to thirty eggs without any union with the male having taken place; it seems clear that the eggs were fertilised within the cloaca.

112868.text: There will usually be a third and a fourth discharge of eggs after a period of seven or eight days, each of fifteen to twenty eggs variously fertilised.

112869.text: The feather-gilled tadpoles will emerge after a gestation period of between one and three weeks.

112870.text: The tadpoles grow into adult newts after just one year and are able to reproduce in their turn.

112871.text: The behaviour observed by Miss Blanche Kistemaeckers of two newts in captivity was somewhat different.

112872.text: At the time of spawning the male approached only one female and pursued her quite brutally; when she escaped from him he beat her with heavy blows of his tail.

112873.text: He disapproved when she tried to take food and drove her away from it; it was clear he wanted to have her just for himself and simply terrorised her.

112874.text: Once he had discharged his milt he threw himself on another female and tried to eat her, so that he had to be taken from the tank and placed somewhere else.

112875.text: This second female nonetheless produced fertile eggs, numbering sixty-three in total.

112876.text: Miss Kistemaeckers noticed that the cloaca of all three animals was very sore, and she writes that fertilisation of the ova of Andrias Scheuchzeri seems to take place not by copulation, nor even spawning, but by what she called the sexual milieu.

112877.text: It is already evident that the two sexes need not come together at an appropriate time for fertilisation of the eggs to take place.

112878.text: This led the young researcher to carry out further experiments.

112879.text: She separated the two sexes; at the appropriate time she extracted the sperm from the male and put it into the water where the females were, at which the females began to discharge fertilised eggs.

112880.text: In another experiment Miss Kistemaeckers filtered the semen to remove the sperm; this gave a clear, slightly acidic liquid which she put into the females water; the females then began to discharge eggs, about fifty at a time, of which most were fertile and produced normal tadpoles.

112881.text: This is what led Miss Kistemaeckers to the important notion of the sexual milieu, which can be seen as a process in its own right, existing between parthenogenesis and sexual reproduction.

112882.text: The eggs are fertilised simply by a change in the chemical environment (a certain level of acidity, which has not so far been successfully created artificially), which is somehow connected with the sexual functions of the male although these functions themselves are not essential; the fact that the male does conjoin with the female is clearly no more than a vestige of an earlier stage of evolution when Andrias reproduced in the same way as other newts.

112883.text: Miss Kistemaeckers rightly observes that this form of mating is peculiar, some kind of inherited illusion of paternity; the male is not the real father of the tadpoles but only an impersonal provider of the chemical environment which is what really fertilises the ova.

112884.text: If we had a hundred newt couples together in a tank it would be tempting to think that a hundred individual acts of mating would take place; but in fact there will be just the one, a collective a sexualisation of the given environment or, to put it more precisely, the acidification of the water to which the mature eggs of the species will respond by developing into tadpoles.

112885.text: If this unknown acidification agent can be created artificially there will be no more need of males.

112886.text: So the sex life of this remarkable species is actually no more than an illusion; the erotic passion, the pair-bonding and sexual tyranny, fidelity for the time needed, the slow and cumbersome act of intercourse, all these things are actually unnecessary and no more than an outdated and almost symbolic act which, so to speak, decorates the impersonal creation by the male of the procreative environment.

112887.text: The strange indifference shown by the female to the frantic and pointless activity of the male is clear evidence that she instinctively feels that it is nothing more than a formal ceremony or a prelude to the real love-making when they conjoin with the fertilising medium; it could almost be said that the female of Andrias Scheuchzeri understands this state of affairs clearly and goes through it objectively without any erotic illusions.

112888.text: (The experiments performed by Miss Kistemaeckers was followed up with some interesting research by the learned Abbé Bontempelli.

112889.text: Having prepared some dried and powdered milt from Andrias he put it in the female’s water, who then began to discharge fertile eggs.

112890.text: He obtained the same result if he dried and powdered Andrias’s male organ or if he took an extract in alcohol or by infusion and poured it into the female’s water.

112891.text: He tried the same experiment, with the same result, when he took an extract of the male’s pituitary gland and even when he took a scraping from the males skin, if taken in the rutting season.

112892.text: In all these cases, the females did not respond at first, but after a while they stopped seeking food and became stiff and motionless in the water, then after some hours they began to discharge eggs in a gelatinous coating, each about the size of pig’s droppings.)

112893.text: While discussing this matter, it will be necessary to describe the strange ceremony which became known as the dance of the salamanders.

112894.text: (This does not refer to the Salamander Dance which came into fashion around this time, especially in high society, and which Bishop Hiram declared to be the most depraved dance he had ever heard described.)

112895.text: The dance took place on evenings when there was a full moon (apart from in the breeding season).

112896.text: The males, and only the males, of Andrias would appear on the beach, form themselves into a circle and begin a strange, wave-like twisting and bending of the upper half of the body.

112897.text: This movement was typical of these giant newts at all times, but during these dances it develops into a wild passion, something like the dances of dervishes.

112898.text: Some researchers regard this frenzied twisting and stamping as a kind of cult of the moon, which would mean it is a kind of religious ceremony; on the other hand some researchers see the dance as essentially erotic in character and seek to explain it primarily in terms of the peculiar sexual procedures described above.

112899.text: We have already said that the female of Andrias Scheuchzeri is fertilised by the so-called sexual milieu surrounding males and females rather than by the personal conjoining of individual males and females.

112900.text: It was also said that the females accept this impersonal sexual relationship far more realistically and routinely than the males who, clearly for reasons of instinctive vanity and greed, try to maintain at least the illusion of sexual triumph, leading them to play a role that involves betrothal and a husband’s authority.

112901.text: This is one of the greatest erotic illusions to be found, and it is interesting that the illusion is corrected by these grand male ceremonies which seem to be nothing less than an instinctive attempt to reinforce their sense of belonging to a Male Collective.

112902.text: It is thought that this collective dance has the function of overcoming that atavistic and nonsensical illusion of the males sexual individuality; this whirling, inebriating, frenetic gang is nothing other than the Collective Male, the Collective Bridegroom and the Great Copulator that carries out its celebratory wedding dance and abandons itself to the great nuptial rite — and all the time the females are strangely excluded and left to squelch lethargically over the fish or mollusc they have eaten.

112903.text: The famous Charles J. Powell, who gave this newt ritual the name, Dance of the Male Principle, writes: “And in this ritual of male togetherness, do we not see the root and origin of the remarkable collectivism shown by the newts?

112904.text: Let us be aware that true animal society is only to be found where life and development of the species are not built on sexual pair-bonding, such as we see among bees and ants and termites.

112905.text: The society of the bee-hive can be described thus: I, the Mother Hive.

112906.text: In the case of the newts, their society must be described quite differently: We, the Male Principle.

112907.text: It is only when the males mass together at the right time and virtually perspire the fertilising sexual milieu that they become the Great Male which enters the womb of the female and generously multiplies life.

112908.text: Their paternity is collective; and for this reason their entire nature is collective and expresses itself in collective activity, whereas the females, once they have laid their eggs, lead a life that remains dispersed and solitary until the following spring.

112909.text: It is the males alone that create the community, the males alone that carry out collective tasks.

112910.text: There is no other species of animal wherein the female plays such a subordinate role as Andrias; they are excluded from communal activities and show not the slightest interest in them.

112911.text: Their moment comes only when the Male Principle imbues their environment with a chemical acidity that is barely perceptible, but which has such power of penetration, such élan vital, that it is effective even when the currents and tides of the oceans have diluted it to almost nothing.

112912.text: It is as if the Ocean itself were the male, fertilising millions of embryos on its shores.

112913.text: “However vainly the cock might crow,” Charles J. Powell continued, “it is to the female that in, most species, nature has given the dominant role in life.

112914.text: The male is there for his own passion and to kill; he is pompous and arrogant, while the female represents the species in all its strength and lasting nobility.

112915.text: In the case of Andrias (and often in the case of man) the relationship is fundamentally different; by the creation of a masculine society and solidarity the male acquires clear biological dominance and determines how the species will develop to a far greater extent than the female.

112916.text: It may well be because of this marked male input to the direction of development that Andrias has so excelled in technical matters, which are talents typical of the male.

112917.text: Andrias is by nature a technologist and tends towards group activities; these secondary features of the male, by which I mean a talent for technology and a flair for organisation, has, before our very eyes, developed with such speed and such success that we would be compelled to speak of a miracle were we not aware of what a powerful force in life sexual determination is.

112918.text: Andrias Scheuchzeri is animal faber, and it is even possible that he will one day surpass man himself given enough time.

112919.text: All this is the result of one fact of nature; that they have created a society that is purely male.”
